summary: Updates the security considerations for the MD5 message digest algorithm and for HMAC-MD5, reflecting what is known about their weaknesses. It updates RFC 1321 and RFC 2104. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: MD5 makes fingerprints of data, but cracks have appeared. This adds warnings to its original instructions.

subtitle: A short update saying MD5 must not be used where collision resistance matters, and HMAC-MD5 should not be chosen for new designs.

tldr.problem: Years of cryptanalysis had shown weaknesses in MD5, but the original MD5 and HMAC specifications still carried their older security text.
tldr.mechanism: This document replaces the security considerations of RFC 1321 and updates those of HMAC, summarizing published attacks on collision resistance, pre-image resistance and HMAC-MD5.
tldr.outcome: MD5 is no longer acceptable where collision resistance is required, such as digital signatures. HMAC-MD5 is not urgent to remove, but new protocol designs should not use it.

today: RFC 6151 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 1321 and RFC 2104.

sections.title: Why the Update
sections.content:
MD5 takes a message of any length and produces a 128-bit "fingerprint" or message digest. The published attacks show that it is not prudent to use MD5 when collision resistance is required. This document replaces the security considerations in RFC 1321.

It also updates the security considerations of HMAC (RFC 2104), which the HMAC-MD5 test cases point to. Where an MD5 checksum is used inline in a protocol solely to protect against errors, it is still an acceptable use. Any application or protocol that uses MD5 needs to state clearly what security services it expects from it.
sections.plainLanguage: MD5 squishes any data into a short fingerprint. Because people found ways to make two different things share one fingerprint, you should not trust it for important jobs.

sections.title: The Overall Verdict
sections.content:
MD5 was published in 1992 as an Informational RFC. Since then it has been studied extensively and new cryptographic attacks have been found. Message digests are meant to provide collision, pre-image and second pre-image resistance.

The RFC states that MD5 is no longer acceptable where collision resistance is required, such as digital signatures. It is not urgent to stop using MD5 in other ways, such as HMAC-MD5. But since MD5 must not be used for digital signatures, new protocol designs should not employ HMAC-MD5. Suggested alternatives are HMAC-SHA256, or AES-CMAC when AES is more readily available than a hash function.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not use MD5 to sign important papers. Older things that use it for a lock can wait, but new things should pick something stronger.

sections.title: Collision and Pre-Image Attacks
sections.content:
Pseudo-collisions for the MD5 compress function were first described in 1993. The first paper to show two collision pairs for MD5 appeared in 2004. Later work made collisions cheap: one cited attack finds an MD5 collision in about one minute on a standard notebook PC, and another claims 10 seconds or less on a 2.6 GHz Pentium4. Collision attacks on MD5 were applied successfully to X.509 certificates, and also to password-based challenge-and-response schemes such as the APOP option in POP.

Pre-image attacks are much weaker. The best result is faster than exhaustive search, but its complexity of 2^123.4 is still pretty high.
sections.plainLanguage: Making two things with the same fingerprint used to be very hard. Now a laptop can do it in about a minute, so the fingerprint cannot prove which one is real.

sections.title: HMAC-MD5
sections.content:
HMAC mixes a secret key with a hash function to authenticate messages. Its analysis is usually done together with NMAC, a closely related construction. The attacks on NMAC-MD5 use related keys, so they do not seem applicable to HMAC-MD5.

A 2009 paper presented a distinguishing attack on HMAC-MD5 that needs 2^97 queries to succeed with probability 0.87 and uses no related keys. It cannot recover the inner key and it is not obvious how it could forge messages. The RFC concludes that the attacks do not seem to indicate a practical vulnerability when HMAC-MD5 is used as a message authentication code. The effect when HMAC is used as a pseudorandom function, for example in key derivation, is not well understood.

So it may not be urgent to remove HMAC-MD5 from existing protocols, but a new design should not include an HMAC-MD5 ciphersuite.
sections.plainLanguage: Mixing a secret into the fingerprint still holds up for now. Still, builders starting fresh should choose a sturdier recipe.
